I know it's clichéd, but I tend to think the common cold works best (especially in cold weather). Doctors would probably see 20 patients a day with something similar, so they're unlikely to overthink it. A bad cold can take you out of action for a couple of days, so requesting a day off isn't unreasonable. The only symptom they can really test is an irritated throat, and you can force yourself to cough for a few minutes before hand. Not sure if it's comparable in other countries, but in Australia there are 'bulk-billing clinics' where you can walk in off the street without an appointment, they charge the minimum fee (which is covered by the government) so they need to see as many people as possible in a day. Generally you only spend 2 minutes in the doctor's office and they're lucky to bother using a stethoscope.

Sometimes I did held my breath while in the waitingroom, by the time I went in, I saw black spots, complained on dizzyness, and had really low blood pressure. My pediatrician prescribed me some multivitamins, and I had the rest of the week off.

Maybe I'm being naive but why would you need a medical certificate if you aren't ill?

In Australia, salaried jobs come with 2 weeks+ sick leave per year. Most workplaces have rules requiring a doctors certificate if you use that sick leave under certain circumstances (viz. if you take more than 3 days in a row, or if you take more than 5 days total in a year, or if you take sick leave against a public holiday or annual leave, etc.). Also, most tertiary institutes requires doctors certificates for "special consideration" (e.g. if you miss a test, exam, or practical; if you need an extension on an assignment, etc.).

Difficult to fake if you are where I'm at (Ireland). If it's an open bleeding wound, you're most likely told to take Ibuprofen (an acquaintance of mine, when he had undiagnosed hairline fracture in his shoulder joint) or Lemsip (me, when I went to the doctor with clogged sinuses and a fever of 38.4C). The important thing is you pay your 60 Euros to see the doctor and are out of the door within 5 minutes without any testing.

The only way to skip work here for fake medical reasons is to go to the emergency room. By my experience, that'll set you back 7 - 22 hours of waiting. The downside: You'll have to stay in the waiting room, and you'll pay 100 Euros to be admitted.

Effectively, yes. I wasn't quite sure how to phrase this as I wasn't sure what they were called in each country (or even whether all countries have them). A standard one is in a letter form, and says something to the effect of, "This is to certify that I saw <name> on <date> and he is unfit to attend work between <start date> and <end date> for medical reasons." And is signed and stamped with the details of the doctors practice etc. Some universities etc. have their own forms to fill out, but it's much to that same effect.
